hero.body: Heat, air and noise pollution, housing: Underlaid cross-references these layers to reveal, neighborhood by neighborhood, where exposures stack up across Paris and its inner suburbs — and sets them beside residents' means to cope.

jargon.iris: IRIS: a small statistical neighborhood unit used by INSEE, typically ~2,000 residents — finer-grained than an arrondissement or commune.
jargon.quartile: Quartile: splits all 2,752 IRIS into 4 equal-sized groups from best (Q1) to worst (Q4) on that indicator.
jargon.cumulativeScore: How many of the 3 sub-scores (thermal, air/noise pollution, housing) are simultaneously in their worst quartile for this IRIS — 0 to 3.
jargon.secondaryResidences: Share of housing units that are secondary residences or occasional dwellings (INSEE, 2021) — shown as context, never part of the score. A rough proxy for the ability to physically leave during a heatwave, which median income alone only captures indirectly.
jargon.capacity: Means to cope: a separate axis, never part of the exposure score. Combines median income, housing overcrowding and the share of secondary residences (INSEE, 2021), ranked across the 2,752 IRIS and split into three equal groups.
jargon.overcrowding: Share of main residences with fewer rooms than the household needs (INSEE definition; one-person studios excluded). In an overcrowded home there's no cooler room to retreat to.

ranking.title: Where the most stacks up
ranking.intro: The neighborhoods of Paris and its inner suburbs where all three categories Underlaid tracks — heat, air and noise pollution, and energy-inefficient housing — are in their region-wide worst quartile at the same time: the maximum score, 3 out of 3.
ranking.tieNotice: Every neighborhood on this page has the exact same score — the order below follows borough, then neighborhood name, not severity. Position in the list doesn't imply anything about how bad one neighborhood's situation is relative to another's.
ranking.footnote: {n} neighborhoods at 3 out of 3. Neighborhoods with fewer than 50 residents (parks, stations, business blocks) stay on the map but are left out of this list. Access to services is no longer part of the score (see the methodology page), and the score moves with each methodological correction — this list is not definitive.
ranking.sameScoreNote: Same score, not the same situation. Across the metro area, highly exposed neighborhoods don't face the same exposures depending on their residents' means: where means are highest — mostly dense, older parts of Paris — heat and old, energy-inefficient housing weigh most; where they are lowest — mostly in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne — heat and air and noise pollution. Every neighborhood below has all three categories in its worst quartile, so they're grouped by residents' means to cope, measured separately from the score.
ranking.group_low_title: Means among the lowest in the metro area ({n})
ranking.group_low_desc: Residents' means — median income, overcrowded homes, secondary residences (INSEE 2021) — are in the metro area's lowest third.
ranking.group_mid_desc: Residents' means are in the metro area's middle third.
ranking.group_high_title: Means among the highest in the metro area ({n})
ranking.group_high_desc: Residents' means are in the metro area's highest third. The exposures are real here too; the map doesn't say which means residents actually use to cope with them.
ranking.group_masked_desc: INSEE doesn't publish income for these small neighborhoods (too few households — statistical secrecy), so they have no means class.
ranking.figuresNote: Each category combines several indicators; one figure per category is shown here. A figure close to or below the median doesn't contradict the worst-quartile ranking — the category's other indicators weigh more there (full detail in the map's panel).

methodology.title: How the score works
methodology.intro: This page exists so anyone — not just someone comfortable reading code — can check what the map is actually claiming, and where it might be wrong. The full technical version lives in SCORING.md in the project's public repository; this is the same content in plain language.
methodology.countTitle: Why a count, not an average
methodology.countBody1: A single blended average would hide exactly what this project exists to show: neighborhoods where several different problems pile up at once. A neighborhood with one severe problem and two mediocre ones can end up with the same average as a neighborhood with three moderately-bad ones — but those are not the same situation, and a smoothed average can't tell them apart.
methodology.countBody2: So instead of averaging, Underlaid counts: for each neighborhood (IRIS), how many of the 3 categories below land in their own worst quartile (the worst 25% of all 2,752 neighborhoods across Paris and the inner suburbs on that category) at the same time? That count, 0 to 3, is the cumulative score.
methodology.notMeasuredBody1: This is called an exposure score, deliberately not a "vulnerability score." Climate researchers usually split vulnerability into three separate things: exposure (is a place physically subject to heat, pollution, bad housing?), sensitivity (how much does that actually harm the people there — age, health?), and adaptive capacity (can they do something about it — the means to act, a home large enough to find a cooler room, the option to leave during a heatwave?). The exposure score only measures the first one. Adaptive capacity is shown separately (below, and in the map's "Exposure × means" view) and never folded into the score; sensitivity isn't measured.
methodology.notMeasuredBody2: That matters in practice. The income-vs-exposure chart on the map shows that exposure, as measured here, doesn't reliably track income — every score band spans nearly the whole income range, including several of the metro area's wealthiest neighborhoods. A wealthy household facing the same physical exposure (heat, noise, an old apartment) usually has more ways to cope with it than a low-income one does. Two neighborhoods can share the exact same score and still face very different real odds of coping — which is precisely why this page never calls that score "vulnerability."
methodology.notMeasuredBody3: The ranking page's split into "Group A" and "Group B" exists for the same reason: it keeps a lower-income neighborhood with a real service shortfall visually distinct from a wealthier one whose score comes from dense, older housing stock instead — same exposure score, different starting point for coping with it.
methodology.subscoresIntro: Every category is built from several raw indicators, each converted to "how exposed" so they combine consistently, then averaged together with equal weight — there isn't yet a principled reason to consider one indicator more important than another.
methodology.thermalDesc: Heat vulnerability index, how many cool facilities (pools, museums, libraries) sit within 400m, how much of the neighborhood is covered by open green/wooded space, and the share of its surface that's artificialized/sealed — built or paved ground holds and re-radiates heat rather than absorbing it.
methodology.pollutionDesc: Combined air pollution and noise exposure class, area-weighted across the neighborhood.
methodology.housingDesc: Share of sampled housing energy-performance certificates rated F or G — France's official "thermal sieve" categories, homes that are expensive and uncomfortable to heat or cool — combined with how sharply a neighborhood's residential electricity use swings with winter temperature (Enedis), a proxy for electric-heating-dependent homes with no cheap way to compensate for heat either.
methodology.thresholdTitle: The "not enough data" rule — and the bias it fixed
methodology.thresholdBody1: A category is only scored for a neighborhood if data exists for a strict majority of its underlying indicators. Below that, the category is marked "insufficient data" for that neighborhood and left out of its cumulative score entirely — never silently treated as "fine" or averaged from whatever scraps happened to be available.
methodology.thresholdBody2: This rule exists because of a real bias found in the original Paris-only data, not a hypothetical one. Two small, non-residential neighborhoods — a Périphérique interchange and a dense commercial block near a department store — were scoring the maximum at the time (4 out of 4, when access to services was still counted), driven partly by an "access" category built from just one or two of its four indicators. Checked across all 992 Paris neighborhoods: among those whose access category relied on a single indicator, 47% landed in the worst quartile — nearly double the 25% you'd expect by chance. Sparse-data neighborhoods were being penalized for lacking data, not for having worse access.
methodology.thresholdBody3: After the fix, both of those examples dropped out of the top score — and the same kind of bias, found again in a milder form at launch, is one of the reasons access to services has since left the score altogether (see below).
methodology.electricalBody1: Housing originally used one indicator: the share of homes rated F or G on energy performance. A neighborhood can now also be flagged by how sharply its residential electricity use swings with winter temperature (data from Enedis, the grid operator) — a proxy for electric-heating-dependent homes with no cheap way to compensate for heat either, not just cold.
methodology.electricalBody2: Both indicators are now required, not just one — a real tightening, not a bug. The two Paris examples above moved again as a result (to 2 out of 4 at the time): both still had enough housing data, but their thermosensitivity turned out close to the citywide average rather than in the worst quartile, pulling their combined housing score out of the worst bracket.
methodology.expansionTitle: Expanding beyond Paris — and a new example
methodology.expansionBody1: Underlaid now covers the full Metropole du Grand Paris "Petite Couronne": Paris plus Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne — 2,752 neighborhoods instead of 992. Most sources were already national or region-wide and just needed their filters widened. Two thermal indicators (cool facilities, cool green area) only ever existed as Paris-specific datasets with no equivalent elsewhere — both were re-sourced to genuine region-wide data (a public pools/museums/libraries register already used elsewhere in this pipeline, and a regional green/wooded-space survey), applied to Paris and the inner suburbs alike, so the sub-score is built the same way everywhere rather than patchwork.
methodology.expansionBody2: A fourth thermal indicator was added at the same time: the share of each neighborhood's surface that's artificialized (built or sealed, from a regional land-use survey) — a structural cause of heat retention, not just another way of measuring temperature. Two Paris-only context facts (street-tree age, street lighting) had no region-wide equivalent and stay explicitly labeled as Paris-only; associational density did have one and was extended to all 143 inner-suburb communes.
methodology.expansionBody3: 32 neighborhoods currently reach the maximum, 3 out of 3: heat, air/noise pollution and housing all in their worst quartile at once — 31 of them inhabited, listed on the ranking page. Most are in dense, older parts of Paris and in Neuilly-sur-Seine; the others are in Aulnay-sous-Bois, Drancy, Champigny-sur-Marne, Le Perreux-sur-Marne and Villeneuve-Saint-Georges. The four that reached 4 out of 4 under the former four-category score are all among them. The Drancy neighborhood has been checked against aerial imagery (see SCORING.md): it borders a large freight rail marshalling yard directly, which visibly explains the heat, noise and near-zero green cover behind its score. The others haven't been checked that way yet — treat every example here as provisional, since the score moves with each methodological correction.
methodology.expansionBody4: This same territory already has a regional precedent worth naming directly: ORS Île-de-France, Ineris and L'Institut Paris Region published "Cumuls d'expositions environnementales en Île-de-France" (2022), a 5-year, 500m-grid study of composite exposure across the whole region, including a case study on Aubervilliers — a commune inside this project's own coverage. It confirms the same underlying idea from an independent source: environmental burdens in this region do stack up in identifiable places. Underlaid's own difference is granularity (IRIS rather than a 500m grid) and a cumulative worst-quartile count rather than a blended index (see "About" on the home page for the full comparison).
methodology.limitsIntro: Naming these limits openly is what makes the score checkable — hiding them would only delay the moment someone else finds them.
methodology.limitIncome: Median income is masked by INSEE for small neighborhoods (privacy threshold): 223 of 2,752 have no published figure. Income is shown for context only — it is never part of the score.
methodology.limitIcu: The heat vulnerability index covers 2,618 of 2,752 neighborhoods; the source dataset uses a slightly coarser grouping that misses full coverage. The other thermal indicators (cool facilities, green area, artificialization) do cover all 2,752.
methodology.limitThermosensitivity: Electrical thermosensitivity is a winter-heating signal — Enedis doesn't publish a summer-cooling equivalent. Using it as a proxy for "can't compensate for heat" assumes a poorly-insulated, electric-heating-dependent home is also hard to keep cool, which is physically reasonable but not independently checked against real summer electricity data.
methodology.limitArtificialization: The artificialized-surface classification (54 of 79 land-use categories) is modeled closely on France's official artificialisation definition but isn't a certified reproduction of it — there's no single published crosswalk from this specific regional land-use legend to the legal nomenclature. It also doubles as a rough urban-biodiversity signal — sealed ground is lost habitat — though it isn't scored separately for wildlife, since no animal mortality or stress data comparable to what's available for humans exists at this grain.
methodology.limitEstimate: The score is an estimate, not a fixed ground truth. Every methodological correction moves the line — treat any single flagship example as provisional until checked against the raw indicators, the way every example on this page was.
methodology.distNote: 32 neighborhoods currently reach 3 out of 3 — 31 of them inhabited, most of them in Paris. Treat them as provisional evidence, not a settled verdict: the score moves with each methodological correction.
methodology.distLastUpdated: Data snapshot as of {date} — the score is re-computed periodically and can shift; a specific example above should always be read against this date, not treated as permanent.
methodology.licensesIntro: Everything here is built from public open data. Each source keeps its own license, checked against what the publisher itself states. Underlaid's code is under the MIT license; the published data (the score and every indicator behind it) is under the Open Database License (ODbL), because two sources — OpenStreetMap and the Ville de Paris datasets — are ODbL, which requires derived data to be shared under the same terms.
methodology.licensesNote: Mandatory citations — INSEE: "Source : Insee". Air-noise map: "Source des données : Cartographie air-bruit établie par Airparif et Bruitparif – http://carto.airparif.bruitparif.fr". OpenStreetMap: "© OpenStreetMap contributors". To cite Underlaid itself, see CITATION.cff in the GitHub repository and give the date of the data snapshot (shown at the bottom of each page).
methodology.capacityTitle: Means to cope: a separate axis
methodology.capacityBody1: The map's "Exposure × means" view crosses the exposure score with a second, separate measure: the means residents have to cope. It combines three INSEE figures (2021): median income, the share of overcrowded homes (fewer rooms than the household needs — no cooler room to retreat to), and the share of secondary residences (the option to leave during a heatwave). Each neighborhood is ranked on each figure, the three ranks are averaged, and the 2,752 neighborhoods are split into three equal groups: lowest, middle and highest third of the metro area.
methodology.capacityBody2: It is never added to the exposure score. Kept apart, the two can be read side by side: two neighborhoods with the same exposure can have very different means to cope with it. INSEE doesn't publish income for 223 small neighborhoods (mostly woods, parks and business areas); they have no means class and are shown as such, never estimated.
methodology.capacityBody3: What it shows: highly exposed neighborhoods don't face the same exposures depending on their means. Those with the highest means are mostly in Paris and stack heat and old, inefficient housing; those with the lowest means are mostly in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne and stack heat and air/noise pollution. Overall, the link between exposure and means is weak — slightly positive only because of dense, older central Paris; in the three inner-suburb departments there's almost no link. And where high exposure and low means do meet, it's concentrated: in Seine-Saint-Denis, 79% of the highly exposed neighborhoods are in the metro area's lowest third of means; in Paris, 2%.
methodology.capacityBody4: What it doesn't show: it measures means, not what households do with them — nothing here says whether a home has air conditioning or whether someone can take time off during a heatwave. The groups are relative to this metro area, not an absolute threshold of "enough."
methodology.accessOutTitle: Why access to services left the score
methodology.accessOut1: Until launch, the score counted a fourth category: access to services. Crossing the score with residents' means showed it wasn't measuring what it claimed, and a series of checks confirmed it for each of its four indicators. It's now shown for information in the detail panel, never counted.
methodology.accessOut2: The social mix of nearby schools describes who lives in a neighborhood, not an exposure — it follows household income by construction. It was the main reason the access category moved with residents' means (correlation −0.52): part of the score was income in disguise.
methodology.accessOut3: Wheelchair-accessible entrances come from a crowdsourced register that's missing for 39% of neighborhoods. Those without it landed in the worst access quartile 29.6% of the time, against 17.6% for those with it — the same missing-data bias this project already had to fix once.
methodology.accessOut4: Pedestrian-path density, from OpenStreetMap, mostly measures how volunteers map sidewalks: Paris draws 53% of its sidewalks as separate paths, Seine-Saint-Denis 17% — elsewhere they're usually noted as an attribute of the street, which wasn't counted. Checked on aerial imagery: the "Klock" neighborhood in Clichy (53,000 residents per km², sidewalks clearly visible) counted 52 m of path per km²; Saint-Ambroise 4 in Paris's 11th, with the same kind of streets, 165,000.
methodology.accessOut5: Travel time to the nearest school, clinic or transport stop is 1.5 minutes or less for 98% of neighborhoods in this dense area, so it barely tells them apart. Access can come back once a reliable measure exists — one that accounts for how busy services are, not just how close — and passes the same data-quality checks as the other categories.
methodology.thresholdBody4: Quartile thresholds are set by inhabited neighborhoods only. The 62 neighborhoods with fewer than 50 residents — parks, river banks, rail yards, stations, business blocks — are placed against those thresholds afterwards: they keep a score on the map, marked "very sparsely populated", but they no longer take up places in the worst quartiles that belong to neighborhoods where people live. They had taken 74% of their places in the worst air/noise quartile, since they often sit along rail lines and expressways.

press.title: Underlaid — press kit
press.subtitle: One-page summary of the methodology, for citation without a follow-up call.
press.whatBody: Underlaid maps cumulative environmental exposure across 2,752 IRIS neighborhoods in Paris and its inner suburbs (Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, Val-de-Marne): for each one, how many of 3 categories (thermal, air/noise pollution, housing) land simultaneously in their region-wide worst quartile. A count from 0 to 3 — not a blended average — set beside residents' means to cope, measured separately.
press.countTitle: Why a count, not an average
press.countBody: A blended average would hide neighborhoods that stack several distinct problems at once — exactly what this project exists to show. Counting, instead of smoothing, keeps that distinction visible.
press.thermalLine: Thermal — heat vulnerability index, nearby cool facilities, green cover, artificialized surface share.
press.pollutionLine: Air / noise — combined air pollution and noise exposure.
press.housingLine: Housing — share of homes rated F or G on energy performance, combined with residential electrical thermosensitivity (Enedis).
press.caveat1: Income is shown for context only, never part of the score (INSEE masks 223 of 2,752 neighborhoods for privacy).
press.caveat2: The heat vulnerability index covers 2,618 of 2,752 neighborhoods; the other thermal indicators cover all 2,752.
press.caveat3: Access to services (travel times, wheelchair-accessible entrances, pedestrian paths, school social mix) is shown for information only, not scored: none of these figures measures access reliably across the whole area (see the methodology page).
press.caveat4: The score is an estimate that shifts with each methodological correction, not a fixed ranking — access to services left the count at launch, which moved the top score from 4 to 3 (see the methodology page).
press.sourceLine: Full methodology and caveats: see SCORING.md in the project documentation.
press.dataSources: Data: INSEE · IGN · CSTB · L'Institut Paris Region · Airparif/Bruitparif ("Cartographie air-bruit établie par Airparif et Bruitparif – http://carto.airparif.bruitparif.fr") · ADEME · Enedis · DEPP · Acceslibre · Ville de Paris · © OpenStreetMap contributors. Licence Ouverte 2.0 and ODbL — published data under ODbL, code under MIT. Full list: methodology page, "Data sources & licenses".
press.meansTitle: Means to cope — a separate axis
press.meansBody: The exposure score doesn't say who can cope. A second, separate measure does: median income, overcrowded homes and secondary residences (INSEE 2021), ranked and split into thirds of the metro area. It is never added to the score; the map's "Exposure × means" view crosses the two. Highly exposed areas with the most means are mostly in Paris (heat, old housing); those with the least are mostly in Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne (heat, air/noise). In Seine-Saint-Denis, 79% of highly exposed neighborhoods are in the lowest third of means; in Paris, 2%. It measures means, not what households do with them (e.g. air conditioning).

about.intro: Underlaid didn't invent this idea — it borrows from tools that came before it, and exists inside an active policy debate. Naming both openly is part of being checkable.
about.orsInerisTitle: ORS Île-de-France / Ineris / L'Institut Paris Region, 2022
about.orsInerisBody: "Cumuls d'expositions environnementales en Île-de-France": a 5-year, 500m-grid regional study of composite environmental exposure across the whole of Île-de-France, with a public interactive map and a case study on Aubervilliers — a commune inside Underlaid's own Métropole du Grand Paris coverage. The most directly comparable regional precedent found: same core idea (composite exposure, not a single index), a coarser and non-cumulative grid rather than an IRIS-level worst-quartile count.
about.orsInerisSource: Source: ORS Île-de-France, Ineris, L'Institut Paris Region, 2022 — interactive map at cartoviz.institutparisregion.fr.
about.adaptBody: The closest existing French tool: 137 agglomerations, focused on officially recognized priority neighborhoods (QPV), built on a 200m grid. Underlaid's difference: IRIS-level granularity (finer than QPV), a public interactive map rather than an institutional report, and a cumulative count rather than a smoothed average.
about.ejBody: US environmental-justice screening tools (federal EPA, California, New York City) that pioneered composite cumulative-burden scoring at small-area granularity. Underlaid adapts the same core idea — count how many burdens stack up in the same place, don't average them away — to Paris and to a different set of indicators.
about.hccTitle: Haut Conseil pour le Climat, July 9, 2026 report
about.hccBody: "France isn't ready": the report that coined "bouilloires thermiques" (thermal kettles) for the worst-affected neighborhoods, published as the state cut the Fonds Vert budget from €2.5bn to €837M and the idea of a "service public de la fraîcheur" (public cooling service) entered debate. Underlaid is built to make that debate concrete at the scale of an actual street.
about.hccSource: Source: Haut Conseil pour le Climat, press coverage, 2026-07-09.

context.intro: Six facts that don't fit the IRIS-level cumulative score — same reason as median income: too coarse a grain to join in without diluting it. Shown here as context, never as an input to the score. Three are still Paris-only (labeled as such below): their source datasets simply don't exist for the inner suburbs yet.
context.lifeExpectancyBody: The 5th, 6th, 7th and 16th arrondissements are among the highest life expectancies in the Paris agglomeration (84+ years). The 18th, 19th, 20th and 10th arrondissements — denser, lower-income — range 79.9-80.9 years (men) / 85.4-85.6 years (women). No equivalent figure was found for the inner-suburb communes.
context.lifeExpectancySource: Source: Institut Paris Région / APUR, ORS Île-de-France.
context.heatwaveBody: in Île-de-France, June 22-28, 2026 — a national record for that week, per Santé publique France's official count. This figure already covers the whole region, Paris and inner suburbs alike; no finer breakdown exists.
context.heatwaveSource: Source: Santé publique France, press release, 2026-06-27.
context.schoolsBody: Citywide plan: 620 schools, 1,200+ portable air conditioners ordered (2026-06-20) — explicitly described by the mayor as "not a structural response to school building renovation". Coverage was uneven: only 8 of 20 arrondissements have a published figure. Hand-compiled from Paris press coverage specifically; no equivalent research exists for the inner suburbs.
context.schoolsSource: Source: arrondissement mairies / local press, compiled 2026-07-11 — see scripts/16_school_ac_context.py.
context.treesTitle: How old is the street canopy (Paris only)
context.treesBody: There's no public planting-date record for Paris's ~219,000 street trees, so trunk circumference (the standard arboriculture proxy — wider means older) stands in instead. The spread is real: {lowName} averages just {lowCm}cm, against {highCm}cm in {highName} — a rough proxy for how long each arrondissement's tree canopy has actually been growing, not just how much of it there is today. Paris's own tree inventory has no inner-suburb equivalent, so this stays Paris-only.
context.treesRow: {cm}cm average circumference, {young} still young saplings ({n} trees recorded)
context.treesSource: Source: Ville de Paris, "Arbres" dataset (opendata.paris.fr), aggregated by arrondissement.
context.lightingBody: A nighttime-visibility proxy only — not a measure of actual safety or crime. {lowName} has the lowest density at {lowDensity} lamps/km², against {highDensity} lamps/km² in {highName}. Paris's own lighting inventory has no inner-suburb equivalent, so this stays Paris-only.
context.lightingSource: Source: Ville de Paris, "eclairage public" dataset (opendata.paris.fr), aggregated by arrondissement.
context.rnaBody: How many currently-active associations are headquartered per 1,000 residents in each commune, from the national register (RNA) — now covering all 143 communes of Paris and the inner suburbs, not just Paris's 20 arrondissements. {lowName} has the lowest rate at {lowRate}/1,000, against {highRate}/1,000 in {highName}.
context.rnaCaveat: Reported per 1,000 residents as the primary figure; per km² is shown alongside since it's a separate, real distortion that per-capita alone doesn't fix — the lowest-density-per-km² communes include the Bois de Vincennes and Bois de Boulogne, whose large park area alone pulls that figure down, not necessarily weaker associational life. A headquarters address also isn't where an association's members live or its activity happens. Read this as one data point, not a verdict on civic health.
context.rnaSource: Source: Repertoire National des Associations, Ile-de-France mirror (data.iledefrance.fr), aggregated by commune; population from INSEE Recensement 2021.
context.layerAsOf: Data as of {date}: the latest refresh of this source failed, so its previous version is shown.

bivariate.intro: Each neighborhood is placed on two separate axes: how exposed it is (the cumulative score, grouped as 0, 1, or 2 and more) and the means its residents have to cope (lowest, middle or highest third of the metro area). The exposure score itself doesn't change.
bivariate.masked: Income not published: few or no residents (statistical secrecy)
bivariate.caption: Darkest = exposures stacked and among the lowest means
bivariate.cell_0_0: None of the 3 tracked categories in its worst quartile, with among the lowest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_0_1: None of the 3 tracked categories in its worst quartile, with middle-range means.
bivariate.cell_0_2: None of the 3 tracked categories in its worst quartile, with among the highest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_1_0: One category in its worst quartile, with among the lowest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_1_1: One category in its worst quartile, with middle-range means.
bivariate.cell_1_2: One category in its worst quartile, with among the highest means in the metro area.
bivariate.cell_2_0: Several exposures stacked, with among the lowest means in the metro area: the combination where making up for the exposure with one's own means is hardest.
bivariate.cell_2_1: Several exposures stacked, with middle-range means.
bivariate.cell_2_2: Several exposures stacked, with among the highest means in the metro area. The exposure is real; the map doesn't say which means residents actually use to cope with it.
